720	The ideal is to educate, not just to shout the truth
721	from the rooftops, the Rebbe said in a footnote. What
722	Rav Yosef says to the Tanna, "my students are sitting here"...
723	What does that mean? You have to come and say, "There are
724	no humble ones, no rabbis, no sages left"? Then what will they think?
725	As he said, they brought it to Rava: "Do not let it be said that none is left, for every
726	creature..." If you are mediocre, what, my children will want
727	to be wicked? You can't. A rabbi can't say
728	the truth about himself. He must respect himself, because
729	there are children here, students here, youths here.
730	He must think how things will be interpreted. That is already
731	an enormous educational lesson in itself, unrelated
732	to the essence of humility. But we want to sum up the
733	questions we asked. First: what is humility? How can one
734	grow great and remain small? What did Moshe Rabbeinu tell himself?
735	How could he stand before Pharaoh and yet be silent before
736	his sister? That doesn't go together so well, right? The Torah
737	praises him, and we see that even
738	HaShem is moved by it. That is, it is
739	an unnatural phenomenon. There is real depth here. Second: how
740	does humility bring strength? We said Moshe was humble, not
741	lowly; Aharon was lowly. Third: how can it be
742	that the humble person is aware of his humility? So humility
743	must be something other than what we think. And we
744	want to develop a very special point: humility
745	stems precisely from knowing your strengths, not
746	from your shortcomings. And let's say it in one
747	amazing, incomparably powerful sentence: when a person succeeds a little,
748	he thinks it is his own. He imagines it is thanks to
749	his talents. When a person succeeds enormously, he knows
750	it is HaShem. When a person earns 10,000
751	shekels a month, he says, "Well, I brought myself to where
752	I got." But when a person overtakes all his friends
753	and sees them from above, what does he do?
754	He looks at the heavens. He says: it wasn't my talents that brought me here. I have the same
755	talents as my brother and my sister. How did I become
756	unique in his generation? Because they placed the crown on me.
757	Moshe's humility stemmed from knowing he was a figure
758	who never was and never will be like him. And so he felt
759	like a man on whom a crown was placed. He felt like
760	a courier carrying diamonds. A courier carrying diamonds
761	doesn't boast. "They chose me. They placed the mission on me. All
762	I need is not to mess up." Moshe's humility
763	did not stem from weakness. On the contrary, it stemmed from knowing
764	that HaShem chose him from among all peoples, from among all
765	other people. And so on one hand it gave him
766	great resolve: HaShem stands behind me.
767	It is not my strength. On the other hand it gave him
768	tremendous modesty. He never felt
769	that he was owed any rights. "I did not create myself,
770	I did not make myself. HaShem chose
771	me precisely because He knew how great he was; he
772	understood that such greatness can only come from above.
773	It has nothing to do with me. HaShem simply
774	chose me." So what was his prayer? That I not
775	fail, that I not spoil it, that I fulfill,
776	that I truly carry out the mission I received. What is this
777	like? Here is a lovely parable.
778	The first Admor of Gur, the Chiddushei HaRim, was a disciple of
779	the Rebbe of Kotzk. He took a small Chassidic group in a small town,
780	Gora Kalwaria in Poland, and made it into
781	an enormous Chassidic movement spanning the world before the war,
782	a mighty one.
783	After he passed away, he had been a truly giant man,
784	an immense Torah scholar of course and a great leader, but
785	materially he saw much hardship in life: of
786	13 children, I think 12 died in his lifetime, and
787	he was left with a daughter named Esther and a grandson, Yehudah
788	Leib, the Sefat Emet. The boy was 19, a youth of 19,
789	and the Chassidim choose the Sefat Emet to replace his grandfather,
790	the Chiddushei HaRim of Gur. He sits on the
791	great seat of Gur's leadership in Poland.
792	He had Chassidim four times his age
793	who had still seen the Rebbe of Kotzk, who had still received
794	Chassidut from the great Rebbe of Kotzk. Once one
795	of the Chassidim came in and said to him: "Listen, the Chassidim accepted
796	you, I accept you too, I have no complaints, but
797	do you feel comfortable? How can you sit,
798	a boy of 19, on this great seat and speak with
799	people four times greater than you, who heard
800	Chassidut from the Rebbe of Kotzk and surely from the Chiddushei
801	HaRim? How do you feel comfortable speaking to them? What
802	makes you fit for this?" The Chiddushei HaRim said, "I will
803	tell you a parable" — sorry, the Sefat Emet said, "I will tell
804	you a parable. A group of mountain climbers climbs Everest.
805	Some fell at the start, some fell in the middle, some split off
806	midway. Two or three of the whole large group
807	managed to reach the top.
808	They reach the summit, panting, satisfied,
809	feeling they have touched the heavens, and they see a small child
810	sitting at the peak, playing in the sand.
811	In one moment their whole illusion shattered. Look, a small child
812	does this. They say to him, 'How did you get
813	here?' He says, 'I didn't get here. I was born
814	here. I was born on the mountain.'" He wanted to hint to them:
815	I did not climb by my own strength. From the start, Heaven
816	gave me, chose me, gave me the strength.
817	So these are not my strengths, they are the strengths of
818	HaShem. But what does he teach them? A wise person
819	is one who does not draw the source of his strength
820	from his own ego; he draws from the One who chose him. A wise
821	person is one who lives all the time with the feeling:
822	HaShem expects something of me. If HaShem
823	expects something of me, on one hand he remains a mensch. It is not
824	his; he is not owed any rights. HaShem
825	chose him, so he remains a mensch. On the other hand, it is He
826	who gives him strengths to succeed more and more. On the one
827	hand, he demands much more of himself.
828	I want to say an enormous point. I saw in the Ramban, I
829	don't remember whether we spoke about it in a class once, maybe
830	yes, a few years ago.
831	It is the idea that a person should understand what his talent is, that a person
832	should understand what his talent obligates him to, that a person should understand to what
833	extent talent is a duty and not only a privilege. I once saw
834	an enormous point in the Ramban, about what is probably the strangest
835	story in the Torah. There is no doubt that if we look for
836	the story that seems most out of place, unrelated,
837	it is the story of Bilam's donkey. What is this story?
